items.readable_text:
Content:
The cross product of two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] is defined as

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b} = | \, \mathbf{a} \, | \cdot | \, \mathbf{b} \, | \cdot \sin\theta \cdot \mathbf{n},]

Content:
where

Content:
- [MATH: \theta] is the angle formed between the vectors when their tails are placed at the same point, and
- [MATH: \mathbf{n}] is a unit vector that's perpendicular to both [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
For example, suppose we have two vectors [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b] such that
[MATH: |\,\mathbf{a}\,|=5,\qquad |\,\mathbf{b}\,|=4,\qquad \theta=30^\circ.]
To compute the cross product [MATH: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b},] we first work out its magnitude:

Content:
[MATH: |c||=|a × b|; =|a|⋅|b|⋅|\sin θ|⋅|n|; = 5 ⋅ 4 ⋅ \sin 30^{∘} ⋅ 1; = 5 ⋅ 4 ⋅ (1)/(2); = 10]

Content:
So, [MATH: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf a \times \mathbf b] is a vector of magnitude [MATH: |\mathbf{c}| = 10] that is perpendicular to the plane containing [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/76be6e5ed10702eed0fad43fc0e7af3a]

Content:
Notice that two possible vectors fit this criterion, as shown above. To decide which of these two vectors we should choose as [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b,] we use the right-hand rule.

Content:
The right-hand rule says that if we extend the index finger on our right hand along the direction of the first vector [MATH: (\mathbf{a})] and have our middle finger pointing in the direction of the second vector [MATH: (\mathbf{b}),] then our thumb points in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a}\times\mathbf{b}.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/72848f25e59c513e35b262c7cabd2394]

Content:
So, in this case, [MATH: \mathbf a \times \mathbf b] is the blue vector.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/571d811d4c733530619d5723eae5e791]

Content:
The cross product is a vector quantity and is sometimes called the vector product. It can be thought of as a function that takes two vectors [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b] as input and outputs a third vector [MATH: \mathbf c.]

items.readable_text:
Content:
If two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are parallel (or collinear), then the angle between them is [MATH: \theta = 0^\circ,] and consequently their cross product is the zero vector:

Content:
[MATH: a × b|=|a|⋅|b|⋅ \sin 0^{∘} ⋅ n; =|a|⋅|b|⋅ 0 ⋅ n; = 0]

Content:
The converse is also true. So, if [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b] are nonzero vectors, then

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{a} \parallel \mathbf{b}
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Expressing this in words, the statement that two nonzero vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are parallel is equivalent to the statement that their cross product is zero.

Content:
Note: The symbol [MATH: \Leftrightarrow] means "is equivalent to," which we sometimes write as "if and only if."

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Vectors Whose Angle Is a Special Angle

Example Prompt:
The vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] has magnitude [MATH: 7,] the vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] has magnitude [MATH: 3,] and the angle between the vectors is [MATH: 120^\circ] and [MATH: \mathbf{n}] is the unit vector that points in the direction of [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}.] Find [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}] in terms of [MATH: \mathbf{n}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We use the formula for the cross product and obtain

[MATH: a × b|=|a|⋅|b|⋅ \sin θ ⋅ n; = 7 ⋅ 3 ⋅ \sin 120^{∘} ⋅ n; = 7 ⋅ 3 ⋅ (sqrt(3))/(2) ⋅ n; = (21sqrt(3))/(2)n.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: The Cross Product of Parallel Vectors

Content:
If two vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are parallel (or collinear), then the angle between them is [MATH: \theta = 0^\circ,] and consequently their cross product is the zero vector:

Content:
[MATH: a × b|=|a|⋅|b|⋅ \sin 0^{∘} ⋅ n; =|a|⋅|b|⋅ 0 ⋅ n; = 0]

Content:
The converse is also true. So, if [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b] are nonzero vectors, then

Content:
[MATH: \mathbf{a} \parallel \mathbf{b}
\quad\Leftrightarrow\quad
\mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
Expressing this in words, the statement that two nonzero vectors [MATH: \mathbf{a}] and [MATH: \mathbf{b}] are parallel is equivalent to the statement that their cross product is zero.

Content:
Note: The symbol [MATH: \Leftrightarrow] means "is equivalent to," which we sometimes write as "if and only if."

Item 9 — Example: Calculating the Cross Product of Two Parallel Vectors

Example Prompt:
The vector [MATH: \mathbf{a}] has magnitude [MATH: 4,] the vector [MATH: \mathbf{b}] has magnitude [MATH: 6,] and [MATH: \mathbf{a} \parallel \mathbf{b}.] Find [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Suppose [MATH: \mathbf a] and [MATH: \mathbf b] are nonzero vectors. Then, [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}] if and only if [MATH: \mathbf{a} \parallel \mathbf{b}.]

Therefore, [MATH: \mathbf{a} \times \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{0}.]
